I don’t think we should limit free speech to prevent hate speech; I prefer protecting speech even when it’s offensive.

Protecting even offensive speech can help safeguard dissent and prevent governments from expanding censorship beyond truly harmful cases.  
At the same time, some hate speech can contribute to real-world harm (harassment, intimidation, discrimination, or incitement), so many legal systems try to draw narrow lines—often focusing on direct threats, targeted harassment, or incitement to imminent violence—while leaving most offensive expression protected.  
A practical compromise is strong free-speech protections paired with non-criminal responses (counter-speech, platform moderation, civil remedies, and enforcing anti-violence/anti-harassment laws) to reduce harm without broadly restricting expression.
I disagree with putting legal limits on speech for hate speech reasons, because I prefer open debate over censorship.

Open debate can be a strong safeguard against censorship and can expose and weaken bad ideas through scrutiny, but it assumes a reasonably safe environment where targeted groups can participate without intimidation.  
Critics of an absolutist approach argue that some “hate speech” functions less like debate and more like coercion (threats, harassment, incitement, or dehumanizing propaganda), which is why many jurisdictions limit those narrower categories while still protecting offensive opinions.  
If you want to avoid new hate-speech laws, a common alternative is to keep robust legal protection for speech but enforce existing laws on threats and harassment, and rely on counter-speech, education, and platform/community rules to reduce harm without state censorship.
I don’t support restricting freedom of speech to stop hate speech; I think the right to speak freely matters more to me.

Valuing freedom of speech highly is a coherent position, especially because once the state has power to punish “hate speech,” definitions can expand and be used against unpopular or dissenting views.  
Even in strong free-speech frameworks, though, most systems still draw lines at things like true threats, targeted harassment, and incitement to imminent violence—limits aimed at preventing direct harm rather than suppressing offensive viewpoints.  
If you want maximum speech protection while addressing harm, the usual approach is: keep speech broadly legal, enforce those narrow existing prohibitions, and rely on counter-speech, civil remedies, and voluntary community/platform standards rather than new criminal speech restrictions.
I prefer allowing people to say unpopular or harsh things rather than having the government decide what counts as hate speech.

That preference aligns with the concern that giving the government authority to define and punish “hate speech” can lead to vague standards, selective enforcement, and drift into policing unpopular political ideas.  
Even so, most free-speech systems still allow narrow limits on speech acts that directly harm others—true threats, targeted harassment, defamation, or incitement to imminent violence—without trying to outlaw mere offensiveness.  
A workable middle path is broad legal protection for unpopular views while focusing enforcement on those concrete harms and relying on counter-speech, social consequences, and voluntary platform/community rules instead of state censorship.
I’m against limits on free speech to prevent hate speech, because I’d rather counter bad speech with more speech than bans.

Counter-speech can be an effective, speech-protective way to challenge hateful ideas while avoiding the risks of vague laws and politicized enforcement.  
Still, many legal frameworks distinguish between offensive viewpoints (generally protected) and speech that directly harms others—true threats, targeted harassment, or incitement to imminent violence—which can be restricted without creating broad “hate speech” bans.  
If your priority is maximizing free expression, a consistent approach is strong protection for unpopular speech paired with aggressive enforcement of those narrow harm-based categories and investment in counter-speech, education, and community norms.
